title: GitLab
description: "Use gitlab.com and self-managed GitLab: issues, merge requests, to-dos, pipelines, releases and webhooks."
icon: i-simple-icons-gitlab

The GitLab provider works with gitlab.com and self-managed GitLab. It can read and write issues, merge requests and commit comments, and it also covers to-dos, pipelines and jobs, commit statuses, releases, vulnerabilities and the webhooks of projects and groups. Merge requests have `kind: 'pull_request'`.

## Authentication

The provider accepts a personal, project, group or OAuth access token:

```ts
import { gitlab } from 'forges/gitlab'

const forge = gitlab({
  auth: { type: 'token', token: process.env.GITLAB_TOKEN! },
}).create()
```

Project and group access tokens act as bot users, so they are the right choice when you need a credential that isn't tied to a person.

If you leave out `auth`, the provider makes anonymous reads of public data. GitLab serves the comments of issues and merge requests only to signed-in users, even on public projects. An anonymous provider therefore reports `threads.comments` as unsupported for them, and reading their events without a token fails with `AuthenticationRequiredError`. GitLab.com also shows full profiles only to signed-in users, so an anonymous `users.get()` returns the login, ID, name, avatar and URL, without `bio`, `createdAt` or follower counts.

## Self-managed instances

To use a self-managed instance, set `baseUrl` to the root of the instance. The provider appends `/api/v4` itself:

```ts
gitlab({ baseUrl: 'https://gitlab.example.com', auth })
```

Webhook delivery logs and redelivery require GitLab 17.0 or later. If you know the version of the instance, pass it as `instanceVersion`. If you don't, `refreshCapabilities()` reads it from `/version`.

## Nested groups

GitLab projects can live in nested groups, so `RepoRef.owner` holds the full namespace path. A project in a subgroup has `owner: 'acme/platform'` and `name: 'widgets'`.

## Notifications are to-dos

On GitLab, `notifications.list()` reads the to-dos of the user. A to-do is either pending or done, and there is no separate read state, which affects how the notification operations behave:

- `markRead()` rejects with `UnsupportedOperationError`, because there is nothing to mark as read.
- `markDone()` marks the to-do as done.
- `unsubscribe()` requires `{ thread }`, because GitLab can't look up a to-do by its ID.

## Event kinds from system notes

GitLab reports changes to labels, states and assignments as English text in system notes, and the provider works out the kind of event by parsing that text. This is why `capabilities.eventKinds` is `'heuristic'`. When the provider doesn't recognise a note, the result is an event with `kind: 'other'`, and the `kindRaw` and `payload` of the event keep the original note.

## Approvals as reviews

GitLab has approvals instead of reviews, so the provider presents them as reviews. `threads.reviews()` returns one review for each approver, with the ID `approval:<username>`. `createReview({ event: 'approve' })` approves the merge request. If you pass a body, inline comments or any other event, it rejects with `UnsupportedOperationError`.

When the user isn't allowed to approve, GitLab responds with `401`. The provider raises this response as `InsufficientScopeError`.

## Release assets

The assets of a GitLab release are links to arbitrary URLs and not files that GitLab hosts, so `releases.downloadAsset()` isn't available. To download an asset, fetch `asset.url` yourself.

## Search

`search.commits()` uses GitLab's Advanced Search. GitLab doesn't report whether an instance has Advanced Search enabled, so the capability is `'experimental'`. On an instance without it, the search returns an empty page.

Commit search accepts free text only. If you pass `author`, `committer`, `since`, `until` or `sort`, the result has a `filter_unsupported` warning. `search.threads()` has no `involves` filter, and it adds the same warning when you pass one.

## Webhooks

GitLab doesn't sign the body of a delivery. Instead, it sends the secret token of the hook unchanged in the `X-Gitlab-Token` header, and the provider compares that header with your `webhookSecret`:

```ts
const forge = gitlab({
  webhookSecret: process.env.GITLAB_WEBHOOK_SECRET,
}).create()

const events = await forge.webhooks.ingest({
  headers: request.headers,
  body: await request.text(),
})
```

The name of the event is in `X-Gitlab-Event`, and the ID of the delivery is in `X-Gitlab-Event-UUID`.

When an update to an issue or merge request changes labels, assignees or reviewers, it becomes one event for each label or person that was added or removed. If there is more than one event, the ID of each is the ID of the delivery followed by `:` and the index of the event.

If you create a hook with `webhooks.create()`, `nativeEvents` takes the names of GitLab's event flags, such as `issues_events`.
